questions.question_text: Who among the following British Governor-Generals introduced the system of Subsidiary Alliance in 1798?

Who introduced the 'Objectives Resolution' in the Constituent Assembly on 13 December 1946, defining the ideals of the Constitution?
The Vijayanagara Empire suffered a disastrous defeat that led to the sacking of the capital city Hampi in the Battle of Talikota in which year?
Within the agrarian society of colonial Bengal, the term 'Jotedars' was structurally used to refer to which class of people?

During the Revolt of 1857, the rebel forces in Kanpur were commanded by which prominent leader?
The princely state of Awadh was formally annexed by the British Empire on the grounds of misgovernance in which year?
Which language did Mahatma Gandhi strongly advocate as the ideal national language of India to foster communal unity?
The Vijayanagara Empire was jointly founded in 1336 by two brothers. What were their names?
The Permanent Settlement of land revenue was introduced in Bengal by which colonial official in 1793?
When was the first comprehensive, all-India population census successfully conducted by the colonial administration?
The occurrence of violent clashes at Chauri Chaura led Mahatma Gandhi to abruptly call off which major national movement?
Following the British annexation of Awadh, Nawab Wajid Ali Shah was unceremoniously dethroned and exiled to which city?
The Ryotwari settlement, a structural land revenue system directly engaging peasant cultivators, was primarily introduced in which region?
In which year did the Cabinet Mission arrive in India to negotiate the transfer of power and establish a framework for the Constitution?
In the administrative structure of the Vijayanagara Empire, the term 'Amara' was derived from a Sanskrit word meaning:
Explain the operational structure and political significance of the 'Amara-Nayaka' system within the Vijayanagara Empire. [30-40 words]
questions.answer: The Amara-Nayaka system was a major political innovation of the Vijayanagara Empire. Amara-nayakas were military commanders given territories to govern. They collected local taxes, maintained an army segment for the ruler, and submitted annual tributes.

questions.question_text: How did the 'Ain-i-Akbari' structurally classify agricultural lands to determine and optimize imperial revenue collection? [30-40 words]
questions.answer: The Ain-i-Akbari classified lands into four categories to optimize revenue: Polaj (annually cultivated), Parauti (left fallow briefly to regain fertility), Chachar (fallow for three to four years), and Banjar (uncultivated for five years or more).

questions.question_text: Why did many prominent Zamindars consistently default on their revenue payments during the early decades of the Permanent Settlement in Bengal? [30-40 words]
questions.answer: Zamindars defaulted because the initial revenue demands set by the British were exorbitant. Furthermore, agricultural prices were low, making it difficult for ryots to pay. The strict Sunset Clause also led to the auctioning of their estates upon delay.

questions.question_text: Why did Lord Dalhousie describe the Kingdom of Awadh as a 'cherry that will drop into our mouth one day'? [30-40 words]
questions.answer: Lord Dalhousie described Awadh as a 'cherry' because of its fertile soil, ideal for indigo and cotton cultivation, and its large market potential. The British progressively dismantled the Nawab's army and finally annexed it in 1856 citing misgovernance.

questions.question_text: State the strategic significance of the Salt March (Dandi March) in expanding the mass base of the Indian nationalist movement. [30-40 words]
questions.answer: The Salt March in 1930 was significant because salt was an essential commodity for all classes. By breaking the salt law, Gandhi mobilized a truly unified, nationwide mass civil disobedience movement, catching the attention of the global press.

questions.question_text: Summarize the primary arguments presented by leaders like B. Pocker Bahadur in the Constituent Assembly for retaining separate electorates. [30-40 words]
questions.answer: In the Constituent Assembly, leaders like B. Pocker Bahadur argued for separate electorates to ensure adequate representation and a meaningful political voice for Muslims. They feared that without it, minorities would be entirely marginalized in a Hindu-majority democracy.

sections.section_name: Section C - Long-Form Narrative & Analytical Essays

questions.question_text: Analyze how the Vijayanagara Empire's urban planning integrated sophisticated water management systems and immense fortification structures to secure its capital. [100-120 words]
questions.answer: The Vijayanagara Empire's urban layout was profoundly shaped by its arid geographic terrain, making water management a critical architectural priority. The Kamalapuram tank and the Hiriya canal were sophisticated engineering marvels designed to channel water from the Tungabhadra river to the royal center and agricultural tracts. Furthermore, the city was secured by seven massive lines of fortifications that enclosed not just palaces and military camps, but also vast agricultural hinterlands and forests. This strategic enclosure of agricultural land within the fort walls was uniquely designed to withstand prolonged enemy sieges by ensuring internal food security, reflecting exceptional foresight in medieval urban defense and civic planning.

questions.question_text: Critically examine the complex relationship between the Zamindars and the peasantry in the Mughal agrarian system during the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. [100-120 words]
questions.answer: During the Mughal period, the agrarian society was highly stratified but deeply interconnected. The Zamindars were a powerful rural elite who did not participate directly in agricultural labor but extracted land revenue on behalf of the imperial state. They maintained forts and armed contingents, solidifying their local dominance. However, the relationship between Zamindars and the peasantry was not merely exploitative; it often involved a paternalistic bond rooted in caste and kinship networks. During times of state oppression or famine, peasants often rallied behind their local Zamindars in armed revolts against Mughal revenue officials, demonstrating a complex structural interdependence balancing agrarian hierarchy.

questions.question_text: Evaluate how Mahatma Gandhi transformed the Indian National Movement from a restricted elite-led campaign into a highly decentralized, nationwide mass movement. [100-120 words]
questions.answer: Mahatma Gandhi radically transformed the Indian National Movement from a restricted elite-led campaign into a decentralized, nationwide mass movement. Through strategic initiatives like the Non-Cooperation Movement, the Salt Satyagraha, and Quit India, he integrated peasants, workers, women, and marginalized castes into the political mainstream. By utilizing simple, relatable symbols such as the charkha (spinning wheel), khadi, and salt, Gandhi effectively communicated the message of self-reliance (Swadeshi) and passive resistance (Satyagraha) to the rural masses. His establishment of grassroots organizational structures within the Congress and his emphasis on social reforms, particularly the abolition of untouchability, successfully forged a structurally unified anti-colonial front.

questions.question_text: Read the extract from the Azamgarh Proclamation (1857): 'It is well known that in this rebellious era, both Hindoos and Mohammedans are being ruined by the tyranny of the infidel English... I appeal to all sections to unite and slay the firangis.' Analyze how this manifesto structurally attempted to forge unity against the colonial state. [45-55 words]
questions.answer: The Azamgarh Proclamation of 1857 was a critical rebel manifesto that highlighted the structural grievances of various social groups under British rule. It deliberately appealed to both Hindus and Muslims, invoking shared cultural identities and historical coexistence to foster unified resistance against the exploitative colonial state and its economic policies.

questions.question_text: Read the extract from Somnath Lahiri's Constituent Assembly speech: 'I see the dark hand of British imperialism hanging over us... we are negotiating a compromise with our former masters instead of establishing a truly independent framework.' Interpret the context of this speech and Lahiri's structural demand for sovereign constitution-making. [45-55 words]
questions.answer: In his Constituent Assembly speech, Somnath Lahiri warned against the lingering 'dark hand of British imperialism'. He argued that the Assembly was a British creation restricted by colonial frameworks. He urged the members to draft a fully sovereign Constitution by breaking entirely free from the structural concessions mandated by the Cabinet Mission.

questions.question_text: Read the extract from the Fifth Report (1813): 'The Zamindars of Bengal are sinking into ruin. Their estates are being rapidly sold for arrears of revenue, and a new class of purchasers, often their own affluent ryots, are acquiring the lands.' Deduce what this structural evidence reveals about the failure of the Permanent Settlement. [45-55 words]
questions.answer: The Fifth Report, submitted to the British Parliament in 1813, was heavily critical of the East India Company's administration in Bengal. It detailed the systemic collapse of traditional Zamindari authority and the rise of local Jotedars, providing crucial, albeit biased, administrative data regarding the structural failures of the Permanent Settlement.

sections.section_name: Section E - Hands-on Location & Map Work

questions.question_text: On an outline political map of India, identify and label the precise locations of five major historical centers: 'Site A' (The imperial nerve center of the 1857 Revolt), 'Site B' (The location of Gandhi's first Satyagraha), 'Site C' (The capital of Vijayanagara), 'Site D' (The British colonial capital before 1911), and 'Site E' (The village where the Salt Law was broken). [50-60 words]
questions.answer: The structural map location coordinates correspond exactly to these historical centers: Site A designates Delhi, the imperial nerve center of the 1857 Revolt. Site B marks Champaran in Bihar, the site of Gandhi's first Satyagraha. Site C locates Hampi in Karnataka. Site D identifies Calcutta. Site E references Dandi in Gujarat.
